content.text:
Read OpenSpec docs, starting with https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/blob/main/docs/customization.md and anything else related to customization. Then use recall and entire to understand how changes are managed in this project in practice.

My general workflow is:

* start a new session, create a branch for the new change (usually on a worktree)
* start with explore or propose skills for a new change (usually, even pure proposal starts with some measurements and validation to ground the proposed design)
* once proposal is ready, create a draft PR with that proposal
* run code review on github to weed out any issues in the proposal
* once it's good, continue with implementation (apply skill), in the same PR
* use unit tests and targeted e2e suites during implementation, create commit "checkpoints" and push to run full e2e tests in CI
* at every "ready" checkpoint, run code review, validate and address findings
* iterate until everything is good and passed manual testing
* use validate skill (I usually forget about it, but maybe it runs as part of archival)
* sync the specs and archive the change on the same branch (before merging)
* bump the version for the release
* squash-merge the PR
* CI on main will automatically release the new version


Such change PRs are often stacked one on top of the other. I'd like every new session to check if there is an existing stack and suggest to open the new PR on top of that stack. this makes work more predictable and prevents major conflicts between branches.

I want to encode the relevant bits of this workflow via AGENTS.md (and the symlinked CLAUDE.md) and the openspec configuration for concrete commands/phases of the workflow.

      Each capability listed here will need a corresponding spec file.

      behavior, so if behavior does not change, no spec should change either.

    template: spec.md

      Create specification files that define WHAT the system should do.

      A spec is a behavior contract, not an implementation plan.

      Good spec content:
      - Observable behavior users or downstream systems rely on
      - Inputs, outputs, and error conditions
      - External constraints (security, privacy, reliability, compatibility)
      - Scenarios that can be tested or explicitly validated

      Avoid in specs:
      - Internal class/function names
      - Library or framework choices
      - Step-by-step implementation details
      - Detailed execution plans (those belong in design.md or tasks.md)

      Quick test: if the implementation can change without changing externally
      visible behavior, it likely does not belong in the spec.

      3. Paste under `## MODIFIED Requirements` and edit to reflect new behavior
      4. Ensure header text matches exactly (whitespace-insensitive)

Stacked on #65 (`feat/marker-text-gap`), which is itself stacked on #64 — **base this on #65, not `main`**. Both rebase cleanly as the stack lands.

## Why

`--to-decor-unit` — one tree level's worth of horizontal distance, and the only number any layer may derive a column from — had been `1.5rem` since Experiment 1, chosen the way the marker gutter was before #65 derived it: it worked.

Tightening the gutter to `0.875rem` changed how it reads. A mark and its text are now one row rather than two things beside each other, and against that the step from one level to the next became the loosest relationship left on screen — the rows tightened and the ladder did not.

## The default widens to 1.75rem

Four candidates rendered across the fixture corpus in both themes and read as screenshots:

| Unit | Step | Reading |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `1.5rem` | 24px | The previous default. |
| `1.625rem` | 26px | Barely distinguishable from it. |
| **`1.75rem`** | **28px** | **Chosen.** A visibly clearer ladder; a four-deep list still spends most of its width on text. |
| `2rem` | 32px | Legible, but chrome starts taking real width. |

Nothing else moves. The gutter is derived from the marks it holds (#65) and is independent of the unit — every candidate rendered every mark on its own column with its text the same distance after it. The floor is `unit > gutter + widest ink-left` ≈ 22px: the old default sat 2px above it, the new one sits 6px above it, so widening only increases the margin.

## The adjustable half — a guarantee, not a feature

You asked for this to be adjustable rather than hardcoded. **It already was**, and that is the interesting part.

Measured on the build before this change touched anything, at `2rem` and `1.75rem`, on both surfaces: every depth's column, every marker, every row's text, the hanging indent, the `.cm-hmd-list-indent` wrapper width, the guide gradient's period, Obsidian's own `--list-indent` bridge, and the footer's rows and group inset **all followed**. That falls out of the grid's own rule — every column derives from one value.

It was also entirely incidental. Nothing asserted it, so the next change to touch a column could have taken it away silently. So the work here is holding it rather than building it:

- **The spec states it.** One declaration at a scope every surface inherits; no surface declares its own; no rule falls back to a literal; no layer holds the value in another form.
- **A new e2e spec applies an override the way a snippet does** — a `<style>` element at the scope the plugin declares at, not an inline style, which would only prove `var()` works — and asserts both surfaces land every row at `depth × unit + gutter` at two different units, plus that the mark-to-text distance does not move with it.
- **Two unused JS copies are deleted.** `DECOR_UNIT_REM` and `DECOR_UNIT_CSS` held the unit as a number and a string for a caller that never arrived. A number cannot follow an override, so the first caller to position something from one would have left that piece on the old grid while every other layer moved — the same shape as the stale gutter fallback #65 found in the footer's heading, caught before it happened.

To retune it, a snippet needs one line:

```css
body { --to-decor-unit: 2rem; }
```

## What the widening flushed out

`52-block-markers-icons.e2e.ts` computed an ancestor guide's column from a spelled `1.5`, and failed at the new default. The failure was the literal, not the geometry — with the unit read from the published property the fold chevron's clearance is exactly what it was. That is this change's own thesis arriving as evidence, and both specs that held a spelled unit now read the published value.

## Verification

- The override spec is **negative-controlled** by pinning one layer to a literal unit: all three of its cases fail, and the output names the offending row and the column it should have been on.
- `decorations` (8 specs) and `backlinks` (7 specs) e2e groups green, vault clean.
- 1075 unit tests, `tsc`, `tsc -p e2e`, `eslint` — all green.
- Screenshot corpus regenerated and read in both themes on both surfaces.

## What OpenSpec customization can actually carry

I read the customization + supported-tools docs, then verified against the installed CLI (`@fission-ai/openspec` 1.8.0, `dist/core/project-config.js`) rather than trusting the docs:

| Surface | Reaches | Hard limit |
|---|---|---|
| `context` (string) | every artifact prompt **and** `instructions apply/archive` | one blob, injected everywhere — workflow noise would bloat every generation |
| `rules.<artifactId>` (string[]) | only that artifact's generation prompt | artifact IDs only: `proposal`, `specs`, `design`, `tasks` |
| `operations.<op>.guidance` (string[]) | `instructions apply/archive --json` | **`apply` and `archive` only** — `OPERATION_IDS = ['apply','archive']`, everything else warns and is dropped |
| custom schema | artifact graph, templates, ordering | artifacts + `apply.requires/tracks`. No git, PR, review, or release hooks |

So OpenSpec has **no hook at all** for: session start, branch/stack selection, explore, propose-as-draft-PR, code review, sync, validate, version bump, merge. Those are exactly the spine of your workflow.

Also verified: `openspec update` **never** writes or deletes root `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` — `legacy-cleanup.js` only strips legacy marker blocks from them. A hand-written root AGENTS.md is safe as long as it carries no OpenSpec markers.

## What the repo does in practice

From PR bodies and Entire checkpoints:

- **Stacking is real and already documented by hand.** #57 base=`depth-contract-property-tests`, #60 base=`fix/reorder-absorption`. But #64→#65→#67 kept GitHub base=`main` with a prose note ("base this on that branch, not `main`") — #65's timeline shows no `base_ref_changed`, so its GitHub diff carried #64's commits the whole time. Two different conventions for the same thing; that's the unpredictability you're describing.
- **Proposal lands as a draft PR, implementation continues in it.** Checkpoint: *"open a draft PR. use feat/<change-name> branch. make the PR description match the intended implementation, not just the proposal. we will work on the implementation in this pr."*
- **Sync + archive on the branch before merge** — `docs(sdd): archive <change> and sync the specs` commits sit on the feature branch, not main.
- **Release:** `npm version` → `version-bump.mjs` → `manifest.json`/`versions.json`; `release.yml` fires on push to `main` touching `manifest.json`. Landed only in #67, two days ago.
- **`config.yaml` has never been touched since `openspec init`** (single commit `eb38ef8`) — `context` only, `rules`/`operations` still commented-out examples.

Three things I hit on the way that you may not know:

1. **The Entire skills are gone.** `.agents/skills/*/` and `agent/skills/*/` are empty directories — no `SKILL.md`. That's why `/recall` fails with "Unknown skill". I used the `entire` CLI directly instead.
2. **`agent/` and `.agents/` are both untracked and neither is ignored** — `.gitignore` says `/.agent/skills/` (singular, wrong name). That's the `?? .agents/` + `?? agent/` in your git status.
3. `entire status` reports Claude Code hooks out of date (`entire enable --force`).

## Proposed split

**`AGENTS.md` (root, ~70 lines, `CLAUDE.md` → symlink) — everything OpenSpec can't reach:**

1. **Session start.** Check for a stack before branching. One command, filtered to your own PRs so dependabot doesn't pollute it:
   ```bash
   gh pr list --state open --author "@me" --json number,title,headRefName,baseRefName,isDraft | jq -r 'if length==0 then "no open change PRs — branch from main" else (. as $p | map(select(.headRefName as $h | ($p|map(.baseRefName)) | index($h) | not)) | .[] | "tip: #\(.number) \(.headRefName) (base \(.baseRefName))") end'
   ```
   Tip = the open PR whose head is nobody's base. Suggest branching there; the user decides.
2. **Stack convention — pick one.** My recommendation: set the **GitHub base to the parent branch**, not `main`+prose. GitHub auto-retargets to `main` when the parent merges and its branch is deleted, so the merged record ends up identical to today's #64/#65/#67 — but the diff is honest while the PR is open. This is the one place I'd change practice rather than just encode it.
3. **Phase map.** explore/propose → draft PR → review → apply → checkpoints → review → validate → sync → archive → version bump → squash-merge, one line each, naming the `opsx` skill per phase, plus the boundary that propose stops at planning.
4. **Repo conventions** worth committing, currently only in my private memory: neutral team voice in docs (we/our), no Claude attribution trailer, decoration/selection follow-ups go to `docs/research/12` and `13` rather than new changes, `minAppVersion` is a tradeoff not a lint to route around.

**`openspec/config.yaml` — the phases it does reach.** Leave `context` as-is (it's product/architecture, correctly scoped); add:

- `rules.proposal` — neutral team voice; state Non-goals; name capabilities against the flat `specs/` layout.
- `rules.design` — point at `docs/research/`, don't restate measurements.
- `rules.tasks` — end with `openspec validate <change> --strict`; every new test gets a negative-control step.
- `operations.apply.guidance` — focused e2e group locally, full sweep is CI's; push checkpoints at ready points; never assert glyph-width pixels in e2e (CI's font differs).

## Overview

The gh stack extension for GitHub CLI creates and manages stacks of pull requests from your local repository. This feature is in public preview and subject to change.

## Key Requirements

The extension requires GitHub CLI (gh) version 2.0 or later.

## Main Commands

The gh stack extension creates and manages stacks of pull requests. Some of the core commands include:

- Initialize a new stack locally with the init command, which in interactive mode prompts for a branch name and offers to use the current branch as the first layer.
- gh stack add BRANCH-NAME to add new branches to your stack
- gh stack checkout to check out a stack by its stack number, a pull request number, a pull request URL, or a branch name
- gh stack modify for changing the composition of a stack (drop, combine, insert, reorder, or rename branches)

## How It Works

A stack is a series of pull requests in the same repository where each pull request targets the branch of the pull request below it, forming an ordered chain that lands on a single branch, typically your main branch. # Agent instructions

## Branching and PR stacks

Every change gets a branch (`feat/`, `fix/`, `chore/`), usually a worktree, and one PR that
carries both its plan and its implementation.

**Before branching, look for work already in flight.** Any open PR whose base is not `main` is
part of a stack, and new work usually belongs on top of that stack rather than off `main` — it
keeps changes from conflicting and lands them in a predictable order. Offer that; let the user
decide.

```bash
gh pr list --state open --author "@me" --json number,headRefName,baseRefName,isDraft
```

Stacks are GitHub's native stacked PRs, driven by the `gh stack` extension
(`gh extension install github/gh-stack`). A stacked PR targets the branch below it instead of
`main`, and GitHub retargets it when its parent merges — so the base is set once and never
maintained by hand.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `gh stack view --json` | the current branch's stack, if it is in one |
| `gh stack checkout <pr>` | fetch an existing stack and switch into it |
| `gh stack init <branch>` | start a stack off the trunk |
| `gh stack add <branch>` | add a layer on top of the current stack |
| `gh stack submit` | push every layer, open or update its PRs (new ones are drafts) |
| `gh stack rebase` | cascading rebase after the trunk or a lower layer moves |
| `gh stack merge` | atomic merge of the stack up to a chosen PR |

Rebase a stacked branch with `gh stack rebase`, never plain `git rebase`: rebasing one layer by
hand leaves every layer above it on commits that no longer exist. `gh stack view` reports a
branch that needs one.

## Change lifecycle

Planning and implementation share one PR, in this order:

1. **Explore, then propose.** Even a pure proposal starts with measurement — ground the design in
   figures recorded under `docs/research/`, not in reasoning about what ought to be true.
2. **Open the draft PR** as soon as the proposal is written, describing the intended
   implementation rather than only the proposal. Review it on GitHub before writing any code.
3. **Apply.** Implement against `tasks.md`, committing checkpoints as each group closes; pushing a
   checkpoint is what runs the full e2e sweep in CI.
4. **Review at each ready point**, address the findings, and iterate until manual testing passes.
5. **Land.** Validate, sync the delta specs, archive the change, and bump the version — all on the
   branch, before merging. Then squash-merge; CI releases from `main` when `manifest.json` moves.

`npm version <patch|minor>` rewrites `manifest.json` and `versions.json` and deliberately creates
no tag: the release is cut from the squashed merge commit, which no local tag can name.

## Conventions

- **Committed prose is team voice** — "we" and "our", never "you", and never session-log phrasing
  ("as we found above"). Applies to specs, proposals, PR descriptions, `docs/`, and comments.
- **Comments explain, never advocate.** No measurements, no restating the code, no arguing for a
  choice already made.
- **No agent attribution trailers** in commit messages or PR descriptions.
- **Deferred ideas go to the parking lots** under `docs/research/`, not into new OpenSpec changes.
- **Read the relevant `docs/research/` notes before touching decorations, selection, or CM6
  extensions.** They exist so a diagnosis is not paid for twice.

## Agent files

`.agents/skills/` holds vendored third-party skills and is tracked; `.claude/skills/` carries
symlinks into it so Claude Code can load them. Everything OpenSpec generates — `openspec-*`
skills, `opsx` commands, Copilot prompts — is gitignored: run `openspec update` rather than
editing or committing it. `openspec/config.yaml` carries the project context and the rules and
guidance injected into OpenSpec's own workflows.
